clue.text: Lorca had a fine translation of his Japanese works

definitions.note: names the writer through the books he wrote

indicators.note: a translation renders words into a new form, so the letters before it are recast

blocks.note: all thirteen letters of these four words are the raw material

explanation.surface: A fine translation of the Spanish poet Lorca's Japanese works, as if he had written any.
explanation.walkthrough: Lorca the Spanish poet is only letters here. LAFCADIO HEARN, of Greek and Irish birth, settled in Japan and wrote many books about it.
explanation.definitionFit: Hearn is famous as the author of books retelling Japanese folklore and describing Meiji Japan, so the works identify their writer.

clue.text: Learns the characters in Braille, initially for an arts course

indicators.note: only the letters making up the word are wanted, free to be put in any order
says the rearranged letters come at the start, before the synonym

blocks.note: its seven letters are rearranged
learns as a verb is a synonym of studies

explanation.surface: A blind student learns to read Braille before starting an arts degree.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's order misleads: 'initially' moves the reshuffled Braille to the front, ahead of the synonym for Learns.
explanation.definitionFit: Liberal studies is the name for a broad general education course in humanities subjects, offered alongside technical training.

clue.text: Station held up during collapse of stout party

indicators.note: in a down clue, holding something up lifts it so it reads from bottom to top
one thing happening during another sits within it, so these letters go inside
something that collapses falls into disorder, so the letters after it are jumbled

blocks.note: STA is a standard abbreviation for station
taken as written

explanation.surface: It parodies the old Punch caption 'Collapse of stout party', here with a railway station held up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Collapse of stout party' looks like one quoted phrase; it splits after 'of', which is the jumbled pair, leaving 'stout party' as the definition of FATSO.
explanation.definitionFit: A stout party is a jocular old phrase for a fat person, and fatso is the rude slang term for the same.

clue.text: Bloomer made by his ragtime band

definitions.note: points to the possessive Alexander's, whose band is in the song title

blocks.note: first meaning: a flowering plant, the umbellifer also called horse parsley
second meaning: the owner of the band in Irving Berlin's 1911 song title

explanation.surface: A blunder made by a bandleader leading his ragtime outfit.
explanation.walkthrough: A bloomer is also a British word for a blunder, which is the sense the surface wants. Irving Berlin's song is 'Alexander's Ragtime Band'.
explanation.definitionFit: Alexanders is a yellow-flowered coastal plant, so it blooms; the same letters read as the possessive name from Berlin's famous song.

clue.text: Aboard the coach, admits the queue sounds a nightmare

indicators.note: we want letters that merely sound like the word before it when spoken
to admit is to let in, so the phrase before it takes the next piece inside

blocks.note: aboard a vehicle is in it
a coach is a bus
the letters C and U spoken together sound like queue

explanation.surface: On a coach trip, the queue sounds like a nightmare.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter Q is spoken 'cue', the same as queue, which is why two letters can stand for the word here.
explanation.definitionFit: An incubus is an evil spirit believed to lie on sleepers, and by extension an oppressive nightmare or burden.

clue.text: It takes an old soldier to dance till dawn, say

indicators.note: say asks for a word spelt as it is spoken, not as it is normally written

blocks.note: a hop is an informal dance
dawn is first light, here in its informal spelling

explanation.surface: Only an old soldier would have the stamina to dance until dawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'till' just places the dance before the dawn.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoplite was a heavily armed foot soldier of ancient Greece, so an old soldier in the historical sense.

clue.text: Chain reaction from splash

indicators.note: the letters are taken out of the next word rather than built up
a reaction pushes back the opposite way, so the letters are read backwards

blocks.note: its first four letters, read the other way

explanation.surface: It sounds like physics: a chain reaction set off by a splash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chain reaction' looks like one phrase; it splits into the definition and the reversal signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alps are the great mountain range of Europe, and a range of mountains is called a chain.

clue.text: The sailor king's rise in simple story

indicators.note: in a down clue, rising means the letters read upwards, from bottom to top
the reversed letters are placed inside the following synonym

blocks.note: a tar is a sailor
R for rex, Latin for king
simple in the sense of unsophisticated

explanation.surface: A simple tale of a sailor who became a king.
explanation.definitionFit: A narrative is an account of connected events, which is what any story is, so the two are synonyms.

clue.text: Banger with a blown pipe making a racket

blocks.note: banger is British slang for a sausage
a bassoon is a woodwind instrument, a pipe that is blown

explanation.surface: A firework banger and a blown pipe together make a terrible din.
explanation.walkthrough: Banger also means a firework, and racket means noise; both are false trails. A racket (or rackett) is a squat Renaissance double-reed instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: The rackett was nicknamed the sausage bassoon because its tightly coiled tube makes it short and fat, so the names are synonyms.

clue.text: Fat prize for Mrs. Cripps

blocks.note: butter is a fat
a cup is a trophy

explanation.surface: A prize for the fattest, awarded to someone called Mrs Cripps.
explanation.walkthrough: Little BUTTERCUP, the bumboat woman in Gilbert and Sullivan's HMS Pinafore, is really named Mrs Cripps.
explanation.definitionFit: In HMS Pinafore the character known as Little Buttercup reveals her real name as Mrs Cripps, so the two names belong to one person.

clue.text: Nona, the windjammer may be called

indicators.note: what something may be called is how it is said aloud, so we want a sound match

blocks.note: a windjammer is a windproof jacket, as is a parka

explanation.surface: It reads like naming a sailing ship, a windjammer, Nona.
explanation.walkthrough: Windjammer usually means a big sailing ship; here it is the jacket also called a windcheater.
explanation.definitionFit: Nona is one of the three Roman Fates, the Parcae, so she is a Parca, the singular of that name.

clue.text: A Belgian sister - the one in the title role

definitions.text: A Belgian sister - the one in the title role

blocks.note: surface reading: a nun or nurse from Belgium

blocks.clueFragment: the one in the title role
blocks.note: setter's reading: a Fleming is a Belgian, and Meredith's novel takes its title from such a sister

explanation.surface: A Belgian nun, cast as the lead in a film.
explanation.walkthrough: George Meredith's novel 'Rhoda Fleming' (1865) is named after its heroine, who has a sister Dahlia; Fleming is the surname that makes her 'Belgian'.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of the novel is called Rhoda, surname Fleming, and a Fleming is a Flemish-speaking native of Belgium.

clue.text: Paddy's temptation

blocks.note: first meaning: a fit of temper, informally in British English
second meaning: a lure used to entice

explanation.walkthrough: Paddy looks like an Irishman's name; it is the British word for a tantrum, and to be 'in a bait' is old slang for being angry.
explanation.definitionFit: Bait is British slang for a rage, like a paddy, and also the lure offered to draw a fish or a victim in.

clue.text: Howls loudly when wreath appears

blocks.note: first meaning: what a hound does when it gives voice
second meaning: the laurel garland given to a victor or poet

explanation.surface: Someone wails at a funeral when the wreath is brought in.
explanation.definitionFit: Dogs bay in deep, prolonged cries, and a crown of bay laurel leaves is called the bays.

clue.text: In America, father and son have food sent up hot

definitions.note: a place in America, standing for the city

indicators.note: in a down clue, sending something up makes it read from the bottom

blocks.note: William Pitt the Elder and his son Pitt the Younger, both British prime ministers
grub is slang for food
H for hot, as on a tap

explanation.surface: An American father and son sit down to a hot meal.
explanation.walkthrough: The city was named after Pitt the Elder.
explanation.definitionFit: Pittsburgh is a major city in Pennsylvania, so it is somewhere in the United States; the definition is just its location.

clue.text: He was drowned at sea - off Caldy Island

indicators.note: off means gone bad or out of order, so the letters after it are scrambled

blocks.note: taken as written
IS is the abbreviation for island

explanation.surface: A report of a man drowned at sea off Caldy Island, near the Welsh coast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'off' looks like a location in the surface. Milton's elegy LYCIDAS mourns Edward King, who drowned in the Irish Sea in 1637.
explanation.definitionFit: Lycidas is the name Milton gives to his drowned college friend Edward King in the pastoral elegy of that title.

clue.text: Grooming aid for a stud

blocks.note: surface reading: a comb or hair product for a vain man
setter's reading: a stud is a stable of horses, groomed with a toothed tool

explanation.surface: A hair product for a ladies' man.
explanation.walkthrough: Stud suggests a handsome womaniser; it is a breeding establishment for horses.
explanation.definitionFit: A curry-comb is a metal or rubber comb used to rub down and clean the coat of a horse.

clue.text: I'm making an example of this suppression of letters

definitions.note: the clue's noun phrase stands for the verbal noun

blocks.clueFragment: I'm making an example of this
blocks.note: surface reading: someone announces they are making an example of a culprit
setter's reading: the short form of I am drops a letter, so it is itself an instance

explanation.surface: A disciplinarian announces they will make an example of somebody.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe in I'm marks the missing A of 'I am', which is exactly the process the answer names.
explanation.definitionFit: To elide is to omit a sound or letter, as in contractions, so eliding is the dropping of letters in speech or writing.

clue.text: Footmen who are familiar with Veronica

definitions.text: Footmen who are familiar with Veronica

blocks.note: surface reading: household servants who know a woman called Veronica
setter's reading: fighters on foot in the bullring, where a veronica is a slow cape pass

explanation.surface: Household servants on friendly terms with a woman named Veronica.
explanation.walkthrough: Footmen here means men on foot, as opposed to mounted picadors.
explanation.definitionFit: Toreros are bullfighters, especially those who fight on foot, and the veronica is a classic manoeuvre they perform with the cape.

clue.text: Stop nursemaid getting in the way

indicators.note: one piece gets in between the letters of another, so it is placed inside

blocks.note: Alice is the nurse of Christopher Robin in A. A. Milne's poem 'Buckingham Palace'
ST is the abbreviation for street

explanation.surface: An order to halt a nanny who is obstructing traffic.
explanation.walkthrough: Stop looks like a command; it is the organ stop SALICET. Milne's line is 'Christopher Robin went down with Alice'.
explanation.definitionFit: A salicet is an organ stop with a soft, string-like tone, related to the salicional, so it is a stop on the instrument.

clue.text: Extra in lead as Lovage

definitions.note: an example of the answer, signalled by as

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the symbol that follows

blocks.note: Pb is the chemical symbol for lead
extra in the sense of additional, another

explanation.surface: It reads like casting notes: an extra stands in for the lead, a character called Lovage.
explanation.walkthrough: Extra and lead suggest film parts; the lead is the metal. Lovage is a herb of the celery family.
explanation.definitionFit: A potherb is any plant whose leaves or stems are cooked as a vegetable or flavouring, and lovage is one.

clue.text: Fruit put me in top form

indicators.note: the words are to be put together in a new way, not as written
to form is to shape into something new, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: all seven letters of these three words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone says that eating fruit puts them in peak condition.
explanation.walkthrough: 'top form' looks like a fixed phrase meaning excellent condition, but 'top' belongs to the letters and 'form' is the signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A pimento is the sweet red pepper or the allspice berry, both botanically fruits.

clue.text: Time for beginners to do as you say

indicators.note: beginners are what come at the start, so we take only the opening letters

blocks.note: the opening letters of these four words

explanation.surface: A teacher telling novices it's time to do as they are told.
explanation.definitionFit: Days can mean a period or era, as in 'in my days', so it stands for time in general.

clue.text: This line sounds almost the best

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a plumb line, weighted with lead, is lowered to sound the depth of water

explanation.surface: Someone declares a line of verse sounds nearly perfect.
explanation.walkthrough: Sounds looks like a hint to hear something; it is the verb for measuring depth.
explanation.definitionFit: A plum is the choicest part of anything, as in a plum job, so it stands for the best of the lot.

clue.text: Cambridge's three-quarters

definitions.note: points to the Backs, belonging to Cambridge

blocks.note: first meaning: the ..., the college lawns running down to the River Cam
second meaning: in rugby, the three-quarter players are among the ...

explanation.walkthrough: Three-quarters suggests a fraction of Cambridge. The Backs are the riverside grounds behind several Cambridge colleges.
explanation.definitionFit: In rugby union the four three-quarter players line up behind the forwards and are called backs; Cambridge's riverside meadows are also the Backs.

clue.text: Hot or cold, a hat is required

blocks.note: C for cold, as on a tap
taken as written
lid is slang for a hat

explanation.surface: Whatever the weather, hot or cold, wear a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot or cold' looks like a pair; the first word is the definition and the second starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: Calid is a rare literary adjective from Latin calidus meaning warm or hot.

clue.text: The end of Dr Johnson's observation

definitions.text: The end of Dr Johnson's observation

blocks.clueFragment: The end of Dr Johnson's observation
blocks.note: surface reading: the last word or conclusion of a remark by Johnson
setter's reading: his poem asks Observation to survey mankind across the globe, ending at a country

explanation.surface: The punchline of one of Samuel Johnson's famous remarks.
explanation.walkthrough: Johnson's 'The Vanity of Human Wishes' opens: 'Let observation with extensive view, / Survey mankind, from China to Peru'.
explanation.definitionFit: The survey that Johnson's personified Observation makes runs from China and finishes at the South American country, its far end.

clue.text: English illustrator retires from fray

indicators.note: to retire is to draw back, so the letters run the opposite way

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for English
Gustave Doré, the French engraver who illustrated Dante and the Bible

explanation.surface: An English artist withdraws from a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: Fray looks like a battle; it is the verb meaning to wear away. The whole of E plus DORE is turned round.
explanation.definitionFit: To fray is to wear down by rubbing, and to erode is to wear away gradually, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Opposed to admitting trainee singer

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so the phrase before it takes the next piece inside

blocks.note: contra is Latin for against
taken as written
L for learner, as on a British L-plate

explanation.surface: Someone objects to taking on an inexperienced vocalist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Opposed to' reads as one phrase, but it splits in two around the inserted trainee.
explanation.definitionFit: A contralto is a woman with the lowest female voice, so she is a type of singer.

clue.text: A blessing, incorporating refined song and dance originally, with neat lines

indicators.note: to incorporate is to take into the body, so the following pieces go inside
originally means at the origin, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: a boon is a blessing
U means upper-class, used of refined language and manners
a strophe is a stanza of a Greek choral ode, sung and danced
the opening letter

explanation.surface: A blessing delivered with refined song and dance, written in tidy lines.
explanation.walkthrough: Neat is an old word for cattle, which is why 'neat lines' fits: BOUSTROPHEDON is Greek for 'ox-turning'.
explanation.definitionFit: Boustrophedon writing runs alternately left to right and right to left, like oxen ploughing a field furrow by furrow.
